schema.name: Full Relationship-Rich Semantic Knowledge Graph
schema.purpose: Detailed semantic map of Python language, runtime, object model, libraries, tooling, implementations, compilation ecosystem, governance, history and influences.
schema.source_policy: Supplied article is authoritative for source-derived claims; no external corrections silently applied.
schema.relationship_policy: Typed directional relationships preserve mechanisms, influence, implementation, usage, derivation, compatibility, governance, distinctions and provenance; generic related_to edges are avoided.

nodes.label: Dynamic vs static typing
nodes.distinction: Dynamic typing defers constraints to runtime; optional annotations allow external checking.

nodes.label: Duck vs strong typing
nodes.distinction: Duck typing concerns supported behavior; strong typing rejects undefined operations.

nodes.label: Statement vs expression
nodes.distinction: Python enforces a rigid distinction; statements cannot be embedded in expressions.

nodes.label: List vs tuple
nodes.distinction: Lists are mutable; tuples immutable and hashable only when their elements permit it.

nodes.label: == vs is
nodes.distinction: == compares values; is compares object identity.

nodes.label: / vs //
nodes.distinction: Modern / performs true division; // performs floor division.

nodes.label: Source vs bytecode
nodes.distinction: CPython compiles source into intermediate bytecode before VM execution.

nodes.label: Bytecode vs machine code
nodes.distinction: Bytecode targets a VM; JIT/AOT/native paths can produce machine code.

nodes.label: CPython vs PyPy
nodes.distinction: CPython is reference implementation; PyPy uses JIT and differs in compatibility.

nodes.label: Python vs dialects
nodes.distinction: Cython/RPython/Starlark-related forms can alter or extend Python-like syntax/semantics.

nodes.label: Annotation vs enforcement
nodes.distinction: Annotations are not enforced by Python itself according to source.

nodes.label: Reference counting vs cycle GC
nodes.distinction: The memory strategy combines reference counting with cycle detection.

nodes.label: with vs try/finally
nodes.distinction: with provides context-manager resource management and cleanup semantics.

nodes.label: Generator vs coroutine
nodes.distinction: Generators use yield; Python extended them for coroutine-like behavior.

nodes.label: Comprehension vs loop
nodes.distinction: Comprehensions are expressions; for is a statement.

nodes.label: Module vs package ecosystem
nodes.distinction: Modules are language import units; PyPI distributes third-party projects.

Python is statically typed
nodes.correction: Python is dynamically typed; annotations are optional and externally checkable.

nodes.label: Dynamic means weak
nodes.correction: The source describes Python as dynamically and strongly typed.

nodes.label: A name has a fixed type
nodes.correction: Names are generic reference holders and may be rebound to objects of different types.

nodes.label: CPython executes source directly
nodes.correction: CPython compiles programs to bytecode executed by a VM.

nodes.label: Python is only interpreted
nodes.correction: The ecosystem includes bytecode execution, JITs, AOT compilers and transpilers.

nodes.label: Lists and tuples are interchangeable
nodes.correction: Lists are mutable; tuples immutable with different key/hash semantics.

nodes.label: Annotations enforce runtime types
nodes.correction: The source says annotations are not enforced by Python itself.

nodes.label: Indentation is cosmetic
nodes.correction: Indentation delimits blocks and therefore carries semantic meaning.

nodes.label: PyPy is CPython
nodes.correction: PyPy is a separate implementation with JIT and compatibility differences.

nodes.label: Snek is Python
nodes.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes Snek as Python-inspired but not Python.

nodes.label: Python cannot be optimized
nodes.correction: JIT, AOT, multiprocessing, native extensions and efficient data structures are described optimization routes.

nodes.label: All implementations have identical semantics
nodes.correction: The source notes alternative implementations can differ in semantics and APIs.

nodes.label: with only applies to files
nodes.correction: with is a general context-manager mechanism for resource acquisition/cleanup.

nodes.label: Identity and design
nodes.statement: Python is high-level, general-purpose, multi-paradigm, readability-oriented, indentation-based, standard-library-rich and garbage-collected.

nodes.label: Origin
nodes.statement: Python was conceived by Guido van Rossum at CWI as a successor to ABC; implementation began in 1989 and first release was 0.9.0 in 1991.

nodes.label: Governance
nodes.statement: Guido left the BDFL role in 2018 and a five-member Steering Council was elected in 2019.

nodes.label: Version history
nodes.statement: Python 2.0 added major features; Python 3.0 was a major non-fully-compatible revision; typing capabilities began in Python 3.5.

nodes.label: Philosophy
nodes.statement: The Zen of Python emphasizes explicitness, simplicity, readability and practical consistency, while remaining a guideline.

nodes.label: PEPs
nodes.statement: PEPs document information, processes, naming and language proposals and are overseen by the Steering Council.

nodes.label: Syntax
nodes.statement: Python uses significant indentation and provides statements for assignment, control flow, exceptions, classes, functions, context management, imports, matching and generators.

nodes.label: Expressions and semantics
nodes.statement: Python distinguishes expressions and statements and supports comprehensions, lambdas, slicing, unpacking, string forms and dynamic references.

nodes.label: Typing
nodes.statement: Python uses duck typing with typed objects and untyped names while remaining strongly typed; annotations may be checked externally.

nodes.label: Built-in types
nodes.statement: Python provides bool, bytearray, bytes, complex, dict, float, frozenset, int, list, NoneType, range, set, str and tuple.

nodes.label: Libraries
nodes.statement: The standard library covers Internet protocols/formats, GUI, relational databases, pseudorandom numbers, decimals, regex and unit testing.

nodes.label: Environments
nodes.statement: Python implementations commonly provide REPLs; CPython includes IDLE and the ecosystem includes IPython, Jupyter and desktop/web IDEs.

nodes.label: CPython
nodes.statement: CPython is the reference implementation, written in C, compiling Python to bytecode executed by a VM.

nodes.label: Alternative implementations
nodes.statement: The source describes PyPy, Codon, MicroPython, CircuitPython, Pyston, Cinder, RustPython and Stackless Python.

nodes.label: Compilers and transpilers
nodes.statement: The ecosystem includes Brython, Transcrypt, Cython, PyJL, Nuitka, Numba, Pythran, RPython and MyHDL.

nodes.label: Performance
nodes.statement: JIT, static compilation, multiprocessing, efficient data structures and native numerical libraries can improve performance.

nodes.label: Development lifecycle
nodes.statement: Python development uses PEPs, community review, GitHub and a release process with incompatible, feature and bug-fix releases.

nodes.label: Culture and influence
nodes.statement: PyCon, Monty Python naming/culture, Pythonic terminology and the influence graph are described.

nodes.sequence: import -> modules -> stdlib -> PyPI -> pip -> extensions
